newsitem.title: ITALY: Is merger fiasco mortal blow to Mediobanca?.
newsitem.headline: Is merger fiasco mortal blow to Mediobanca?.

text.p: After two humiliating fiascos in a row for the investment bank that has ruled Italian business for half a century, the unthinkable is now being said out loud.
Maybe Mediobanca's reign is drawing to a close.

The shock collapse on Saturday of a planned mega-merger between textile group Marzotto and industrial holding company HPI, crafted by Mediobanca's 90-year-old honorary chairman Enrico Cuccia, was seen as a death knell for the bank and its ways.
"What really happened on Saturday morning was that Mediobanca was dealt a mortal blow," Giuseppe Turani, an expert on the group, wrote in La Repubblica.

"After the disaster of 'SuperGemina' and Marzotto's 'no', (Mediobanca) is no longer the number one crossroads of Italian capitalism. It's just a collection of rooms where old gentlemen try to defend a power that the markets don't accept any more."

Cuccia's touch failed him embarrassingly in 1995 when the "SuperGemina" deal to bundle the interests of financial holding company Gemina with the former Ferruzzi agri-chemicals empire was scrapped after huge losses at a Gemina unit came to light.

That unprecedented disaster for the once-infallible Mediobanca was a bitter pill for Cuccia and his empire's reputation was undermined further by poorly performing shares and waning involvement in Italy's privatisation programme.

"Out of style" concluded communist daily Il Manifesto above front-page pictures of Cuccia and Fiat boss Cesare Romiti after the failure of the Marzotto-HPI deal that was to have created an international fashion powerhouse.

Fiat, one of the family-run blue-chip companies at the centre of Cuccia's way of doing business, was to have held a 17.3 percent stake in the merged company, Gruppo Industriale Marzotto, which had earned the nickname "Big GIM".

Cuccia, an obsessively secretive Sicilian, has effectively run Mediobanca since its foundation in 1946 and helped bolster the power of Italy's top industrial dynasties by spinning a web of corporate alliances.

Commentators said Marzotto's sudden decision to pull out of the merger with just two months to go reflected fears that the family would lose control of their business after more than 160 years -- and at the expense of another family empire, Fiat.

"The Marzottos have realised that in the union with Mediobanca and Fiat, they would have disappeared," Turani wrote in La Repubblica. The Marzotto family had been due to hold a 12.4 percent stake in GIM and Mediobanca 10.5 percent.
Cuccia has bounced back from failures before -- such as the ill-fated union between tyre maker Pirelli and Dunlop which came unstuck in 1981.
But commentators said the bank, whose discreet headquarters in Via Filodrammatici are just behind Milan's La Scala opera house, was now looking out of step with modern business culture.
But some commentators warned it would be wrong to write Cuccia off just yet.
"Cuccia's stubborn and he'll try again, hoping to make it third time lucky," L'Unita newspaper predicted.
